title: After Paris: his own groups at the Rendezvous and in Columbus
summary: Back home, Moore led groups in Philadelphia and Columbus, and joined the Metropole when it became a jazz room.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: All right, so after the Paris Festival --
When I got back from Paris, I remember Lee Guber telling me to bring my group over to the Rendezvous in Philadelphia. So I got together Lloyd Phillips on piano, Freddie Moore on drums, Omar
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943

Simeon was with me in Rendezvous. We did pretty good, very good, very nice engagement. Then we went back to New York after Philadelphia and I still kicked around Central Plaza, Stuyvesant and then I made a group, formed a group, I got a contract to head a band to take to Columbus, Ohio. In the band I had Buck Clayton, the drummer this time was Kansas Fields, Red Richards and Buster Bailey again and we had a nice engagement in Columbus.
What were some of the selections that you performed, that your band performed? You played "Panama" which is a favorite of yours. "Stardust." Things that you liked to play.

No, I had left "Stardust." I left "Stardust," I played mostly mind you for Sidney Bechet I was playing the traditional tunes, Buck knew must of the tunes and Buck did his special number. I featured everyone in the band. I didn't take the whole cheese, you know. I wasn't the whole cheese. I featured Buster Bailey in the "St. Louis Blues." He used to do this -- wailed a lone note for the longest time possible, he used that ending -- in-breathing --
Then Buck did his thing, I featured

Kansas also. Then Red played his thing and I understand right now, this taping right now, he's in Europe, in Paris. That's nice. That's great. He's doing fine. I talked to Mrs. Richards and had them over to the house and, anyway, following the frolics in Columbus I came back and low and behold, in between, back to the Stuyvesant and Central Plaza the Metropole Cafe on 48th and Broadway had changed its policy to jazz and I was one of the first bands that opened that place into jazz. The line-up was Jimmy McPartland, Bud Freeman, on tenor, and on piano we had -- who was playing drums -- George Wettling was playing drums, Dick Cary and we had Milt Hinton.
